metadata.source_title: Evolution and Selection of Quantitative Traits

blocks.content: Consider the change in the frequency $p$ of allele $A$ over one generation, $ p = p' - p$. As shown in [[SEE_TABLE:5.1]], the number of AA individuals following selection is proportional to $p^2 W_{AA}$, the frequency of AA genotypes before selection multiplied by their genotypic fitness. To ensure that post-selection frequencies sum to one, we divide this proportion by a normalization constant, the mean population fitness (the average fitness of a randomly chosen individual), [[SEE_FORMULA:5.1a]]

Proceeding similarly for the other genotypes allows us to fill out the entries in [[SEE_TABLE:5.1]]. From these new genotypic frequencies, the frequency of A after selection is $$ p^{\prime}=freq(AA after selection)+\frac{1}{2}freq(Aa after selection) $$ and applying the results in [[SEE_TABLE:5.1]] gives the expected change in the frequency of A as [[SEE_FORMULA:5.1b]]

This equation can also be expressed using the relative fitnesses $ W_{ij} / \overline{W} $ , abbreviated as $ w_{ij} $ , with mean fitness then scaling to $ \overline{w}=1 $ . Throughout, we will adhere to a notation whereby upper-case W corresponds to some absolute measure of fitness, and lower-case w corresponds to relative fitness.

If we assign the genotypes $ aa:Aa:AA $ fitnesses of $ 1:1+s(1+h):1+2s $, Equation 5.1b becomes [[SEE_FORMULA:5.1c]] As shown in Figure 5.1, a graph of $ p $ as a function of p provides a useful description of the allele-frequency dynamics under selection. In particular, allele frequencies that satisfy

$ \Delta p=0 $ (i.e., no allele-frequency change after selection) are called equilibrium frequencies, which we denote by $ \widehat{p} $ . Regardless of the values of s or h, trivial boundary equilibria exist when only one allele is present $ (\widehat{p}=0 $ or 1). Equation 5.1c shows that an internal equilibrium, in which both alleles are segregating, requires $ 1+h(1-2\widehat{p})=0 $ , which yields $ \widehat{p}=(1+h)/(2h) $ . Thus either $ h>1 $ (overdominance) or $ h<-1 $ (underdominance) is required to ensure $ 0<\widehat{p}<1 $ . However, the equilibrium behavior is very different in these two cases. The situation $ h>1 $ represents a stable equilibrium, in which following a small perturbation from $ \widehat{p} $ , selection returns the allele frequency to $ \widehat{p} $ (Figure 5.1C). In contrast, with h < -1, there is an unstable equilibrium, selection sends the allele frequency away from $ \widehat{p} $ which following a small perturbation (Figure 5.1D).

Example 5.1. Letting $ p = (A) $, what is $ p $ when $ W_{AA} = 1 + 2s $, $ W_{Aa} = 1 + s $, and $ W_{aa} = 1 $? These are additive fitnesses, with each copy of allele A adding an amount $ s $ to the fitness. In this case, mean fitness simplifies to $ = 1 + 2sp $ (there is an average of $ 2p $ A alleles per individual, each of which increments fitness by $ s $), and applying Equation 5.1c (setting $ h = 0 $) yields $$ \Delta p=\frac{sp(1-p)}{1+2sp} $$
Noting that a first-order Taylor expansion (in s) yields $ 1/(1+2sp)=1-2sp+O(s^{2}) $, for $ |s| $ small, we have [[SEE_FORMULA:5.2b]]
The notation $ O(s^2) $ denotes terms of order $ s^2 $, which are negligible for $ |s| 1 $.

The only equilibrium allele frequencies under this model are $ \widehat{p}=0 $ and $ \widehat{p}=1 $ . If A is favored by selection (s>0), then $ \Delta p>0 $ for 0<p<1 and the frequency of A increases to one, regardless of the starting point (Figure 5.1A). Here $ \widehat{p}=1 $ is a stable equilibrium point while $ \widehat{p}=0 $ is unstable, because if even a few copies of A are introduced, selection drives them to fixation. In contrast, if allele a is favored (s<0), the frequency of allele A declines to zero regardless of the starting point and $ \widehat{p}=0 $ is stable, while $ \widehat{p}=1 $ is unstable.
